transcript:
[00:00] Alex Chen: ok hey everyone thanks for joining, um we'll go ahead and get started. alex from Redwood, priya's on the call as well, she'll drive the deep technical parts.
[00:34] Maria Gonzalez: thanks Alex, yeah we got the calendar. quick reminder our goal today is we want to understand how to plan capacity for our payment fraud inline models, we hit spikes during settlement windows, and we need predictable P99 latency under 500ms ideally.
[01:12] Priya Sharma: great, that helps. can you give us a traffic profile, like QPS, burst factor, average sequence length? even ballpark numbers help.
[01:45] Tom Baker: sure we currently see an avg of 60 QPS, spikes up to 450 for a few minutes, seq lengths vary, enum: most requests are short 128 tokens, some longer sessions up to 1024 tokens when we do context enrichment.
[02:05] Alex Chen: ok that's helpful. for those burst patterns there are two levers: reserved GPUs (predictable throughput) plus a burst pool for short peaks; or a hosted mode with aggressive scaling but it's harder to guarantee P99.
[03:10] Maria: our security team is leaning toward VPC/private deployments, we need SOC2 plus KMS integration and no data egress outside region. can Redwood Dedicated support that?
[03:48] Priya: yes Redwood Dedicated and Redwood Private both support VPC peering and customer managed KMS. there are some config steps for firewall rules and peering; Jamal we'll follow up on the egress list.
[04:12] Jamal Reed: yeah i'll share the egress list, and we need to understand the peering IPs and subnets.
[05:00] Priya: from the runtime perspective, the important bits for capacity are: model size, KV cache hit rate, batching behavior, and quantization config. each affects per-token latency differently.
[05:34] Alex: one misconception we see is people assume bigger batch means lower cost but latency balloons for small tails; so we tune dynamic batching thresholds to respect P95 and P99.
[06:10] Maria: can you walk through queueing model options? we've been thinking about simple FIFO vs priority queues for high-value transactions.
[06:42] Priya: yeah so simple FIFO is straightforward, but you can do a priority queue where high-value requests bypass the batch window or use a low-latency path. another pattern is two-tier pools: reserved for low-latency critical traffic, cheaper spot-like burst for best-effort. on the runtime we support request tags to route by policy.
[07:20] Tom: how does that routing work under contention, e.g. if reserved pool is saturated?
[07:40] Priya: we have automatic fallback - requests can be routed to a compatible model variant (smaller quantized model) or to a different region if cross-region latency isn't prohibitive. fallback policies can be per-route. there is also queue length caps and admission control so tails don't blow up.
[08:15] Maria: what's the expected P99 impact if we allow fallbacks to a quantized variant?
[08:38] Priya: depends on model and quantization level; in our benchmarks a 4-bit quantized variant typically adds 5-12ms server-side but can reduce compute demand by 2-3x. however sometimes CPU scheduling for quantized kernels can add jitter if not warmed. we'll share the bench sheet.
[09:10] Alex: note that cold-starts for a shard that's been scaled to zero can add 100s of ms, so for tight P99s you want at least a small hot pool. that's why reserved GPUs are common.
[09:45] Jamal: what about KV cache sizing? we have many users and want to avoid cold KV misses during bursts.
[10:10] Priya: KV cache hit rate is huge for long-context models because a hit avoids many transformer layers. sizing depends on unique prefix count. for Atlas's workload if you have many users with largely disjoint contexts you need larger KV. we recommend tracking distinct context counts and setting a cache TTL and LRU policy; also we can do per-tenant cache partitions in Dedicated to reduce eviction churn.
[11:05] Maria: if we partition caches per-tenant does that increase memory footprint a lot?
[11:28] Priya: yes some overhead, but it's usually worth it for predictable latency. you can combine partitioning with a small common cache for shared prompts.
[12:00] Alex: let's talk numbers. given 60 QPS steady and spikes to 450, with 128 token avg, you can expect tokens/sec in the thousands, so you typically reserve 2-4 GPUs (model-dependent) and add a burst pool that can add another 4 GPUs for short periods. these are rough - we'll put exact numbers in the bench sheet.
[12:40] Tom: how do burst policies work? is there autoscaling cooldowns? we don't want rapid spin-ups that cost a lot.
[13:05] Priya: yes cooldowns configurable. burst policy patterns: 1) pre-warmed burst capacity (always-on but idle) 2) rapid scale-up up to a cap with cooldowns and cost-smoothing, 3) queue-based throttling where excess requests queue and we return a 202/async token. you can combine them; many customers do reserved + prewarm + short autoburst.
[13:48] Maria: is there support for async inference? some of these spikes are non-critical and could be batched offline.
[14:10] Alex: absolutely, we support async job queues and webhooks for completion. that helps smooth peaks and saves cost.
[15:00] Priya: another nuance: batching gains diminish with shorter sequences and more KV hit patterns. for your short 128-token requests, dynamic batching can still help but you must keep batch windows small to avoid latency.
[15:45] Tom: can Redwood enforce per-route SLOs, like route A must be P99 < 500ms, route B best-effort?
[16:10] Priya: yes per-route SLOs and you can pin routes to different pools. we also expose token-level latency metrics and per-route dashboards in the console for troubleshooting.
[17:00] Maria: let's talk price. reserved GPUs monthly commitment vs pay-as-you-go, can you share a sample calc?
[17:30] Alex: we'll send a pricing sheet but in general reserved gives 40-60% lower unit cost vs on-demand, depending on commit. also quantization and batching reduce unit cost. we can model your 30-day traffic to show TCO.
[18:05] Jamal: for VPC/private, what network egress do you need? and how do we do KMS?
[18:28] Priya: we'll provide a small set of egress IPs for peering, and KMS/HSM integrates via customer-managed keys — you maintain the key, Redwood keeps encrypted at rest. we also emit audit logs to a customer SIEM on request.
[19:00] Maria: any compliance caveats for on-prem?
[19:20] Alex: on-prem package can be air-gapped, but you lose some managed telemetry; we provide a compliance pack and assist during SOC2/ISO audits.
[20:05] Tom: okay, back to queuing, are there queue length caps we should configure to avoid buildup?
[20:30] Priya: yes you can set queue max size and max wait time; once exceeded we either reject or route to async. for payments you'd likely prefer reject with a fast fail or route to a lighter model.
[21:15] Maria: curious about tail latencies with batching - do you expose percentiles per batch size?
[21:40] Priya: yes, per-batch metrics, and we correlate with KV hit rates. often high tail correlates with cache churn and cold model shards.
[22:20] Alex: small aside — some customers see jitter from underlying NVLink contention when many shards co-locate. we tune scheduling to avoid high co-located hot shards.
[23:05] Jamal: what's the typical warm-up time for a quantized shard?
[23:30] Priya: warm-up often just a few seconds of inference traffic but depends on kernel JITs; some runtimes do a minute for heavy initialization. we usually prewarm for critical routes.
[24:10] Maria: for the pilot can we get a 48-72 hour run with traffic replay?
[24:40] Alex: yes we can provision a small dedicated test pool and replay your traffic, run bench scripts, and produce a results deck. we'll need the traffic profile and a sample payload.
[25:15] Tom: what about quantization regressions for our accuracy bar? we require minimal degradation.
[25:40] Priya: we run evals tied to prompt sets; we can test 8-bit vs 4-bit with your evals and only recommend quant levels that meet your accuracy SLOs. Redwood Optimize can recommend configs automatically.
[26:20] Maria: how do you suggest we start — reserve too many GPUs or risk underprovisioning?
[26:40] Alex: start with a small reserved baseline sized for typical load plus short pre-warm for bursts, run the replay pilot, then iterate. you can also set budget caps. we usually model costs for 3 scenarios: conservative reserved, hybrid reserved+burst, and fully dynamic.
[28:00] Priya: also note that some customers use a headroom percentage: reserve 70-80% of steady and allow bursts to autoscale the last 20-30% with strict cooldowns. this balances cost vs latency.
[29:10] Maria: ok are there any gotchas with our cloud provider? we're on Azure in east-us-2.
[29:40] Priya: we support Azure regions, but GPU SKUs differ; some optimized kernels are better on A100-equivalents vs older SKUs. we'll map model to best SKU. also region capacity for burst GPUs can be limited, so reserved capacity is recommended if you need guaranteed bursts.
[30:15] Tom: can Redwood provide an SLA for Dedicated?
[30:35] Alex: yes Dedicated has SLA-backed uptime and latency targets in enterprise plan; we'll share contract language.
[31:00] Maria: talk me through an example admission control/queueing policy for high-value payment checks.
[31:20] Priya: e.g., policy: requests flagged high-value go to reserved pool with immediate admission and a small batch window (5-10ms); standard requests go to pooled pool with 25ms batch window. if reserved pool exhausted, either reject or fallback to quantized model. we can implement per-route fallback thresholds.
[32:05] Jamal: performance of quantized kernels on our chosen SKU — any guidance?
[32:30] Priya: we'll provide bench numbers; some older GPUs have slower int kernels. again we'll include a mapping table in the bench sheet.
[33:10] Alex: note for P99 under 500ms you want to budget headroom for GC, network, and queueing. we usually budget 20-30% overhead.
[34:00] Maria: ok can you share the bench sheet now?
[34:20] Priya: sharing - Link: [benchmark spreadsheet] (internal link). it's got per-model token/sec, latency by batch size, quantization deltas, and suggested reserved GPU counts.
[35:05] Tom: great, i see a row where 4-bit reduced GPU need from 4 to 1 but added 8ms latency - that seems worth it for batch jobs but not for critical payments.
[35:30] Priya: exactly - that's the tradeoff. some customers keep two variants behind a routing policy.
[36:00] Maria: are there controls to evict long-running KV entries? we have some sessions that never end.
[36:20] Priya: TTL + LRU and per-tenant quotas. we can also suggest heuristics to drop very old contexts.
[37:10] Jamal: for the pilot how soon can you get us a dedicated test pool?
[37:30] Alex: we can usually provision within 48 hours for small pools, longer for large reserved capacity. we'll coordinate with your infra.
[38:00] Tom: do you have examples of cost modeling for hybrid setups?
[38:20] Alex: yes we'll include cost model scenarios in the follow-up and a sample excel.
[39:10] Maria: anything else we're missing?
[39:30] Priya: monitoring — set up alerting on P95/P99, Queue length, KV miss rate. also configure tracing to see per-request model variant and batch size.
[40:05] Alex: and we'll share a template pilot plan: traffic replay steps, success criteria (P99 < 500ms for critical route, less than 2% accuracy delta for quantized models), and cutover checklist.
[41:00] Tom: one security Q — does Redwood maintain customer audit logs for inference requests?
[41:20] Priya: yes we can stream audit logs to your SIEM, with appropriate redaction controls for PII.
[42:00] Maria: ok let's recap next steps.
[42:10] Alex: recap: Redwood sends pricing + bench sheet + pilot plan; Atlas provides traffic profile and sample payloads; schedule pilot planning meeting. action items recorded.
[43:00] Jamal: quick nit — are there examples of queue-backed async patterns?
[43:20] Priya: yes we have a pattern doc and example webhook flow, we'll drop it in the folder.
[44:05] Maria: thanks everyone, this was helpful.
[44:25] Alex: great, thanks — we'll follow up with the artifacts.
[44:40] Priya: one last thing: beware of cold sharding in multi-tenant env, we recommend per-tenant soft affinity if you have hotspots.
[45:10] Tom: noted. thanks.
[46:00] [End of recording]
